claims.statement: The Met gives Hammurabi's reign as about 1792–1750 BCE; the French Ministry of Culture gives 1792–1750 BCE.

start.original: ca. 1792 B.C. (Met); became king in 1792 (French Ministry of Culture)

end.original: ca. 1750 B.C. (Met); ruled until 1750 (French Ministry of Culture)

claims.disputeNote: The Met qualifies its conventional dates as approximate; alternate absolute chronologies were not examined in this calibration.

value.text: expanded Babylonian control across much of southern Mesopotamia and unified much of Mesopotamia

claims.statement: The Met says Hammurabi expanded control in the south and unified much of Mesopotamia.
claims.disputeNote: The museum overview does not detail the sequence or degree of control; this is a broad summary, not a boundary claim.

claims.statement: During Hammurabi's expansion, he destroyed King Zimri-Lim's palace at Mari.
claims.disputeNote: The Met directly identifies Hammurabi as destroying Zimri-Lim’s palace. The Ministry page describes Mari as defeated and destroyed in 1761 BCE, but is contextual support for the palace-specific assertion.

value.text: Tell Hariri in the middle valley of the Syrian Euphrates is the site of ancient Mari

claims.statement: The French archaeological mission identifies Tell Hariri, in the middle valley of the Syrian Euphrates, as the site of ancient Mari.

value.text: Thousands of tablets were found in the Great Royal Palace

claims.statement: Excavations found thousands of tablets in Mari's Great Royal Palace.
claims.disputeNote: This speaks to the palace archive, not all activity or literacy in the city.

value.text: A massive archive of cuneiform tablets provides information about contemporary political events

claims.statement: The Met describes Mari's palace archive as a source for contemporary political events.
claims.disputeNote: This is a modern museum summary; individual archival texts and their dates have not been examined here.

value.text: House F in Nippur, excavated in the early 1950s, is widely believed to have been a scribal school; tablets document an educational curriculum

claims.statement: A University of Chicago publication examines Old Babylonian education through House F at Nippur, widely believed to have been a scribal school, and the curriculum documented by tablets found there.
claims.disputeNote: The source itself says 'widely believed'; House F's identification as a school is not presented as certain.

claims.statement: The House F publication frames its study as education in the Old Babylonian period.
claims.disputeNote: The consulted book-description page does not provide a narrower date range for the specific tablets or school activity; entry dates remain unknown.

evidence.note: The Met explicitly gives Hammurabi’s reign as ca. 1792–1750 B.C.; start and end are represented separately in the claim validity.

evidence.locator: Object record, title/date and Places and dates (page lines 237–241, 288–294)
evidence.note: Louvre dates the stele to Hammurabi’s dynasty (-1792 to -1750); this is artefact dating and context for the reign, not direct evidence for its endpoints.
French Ministry page says he became king in 1792 and ruled until 1750.
The Met calls Hammurabi king of Babylon.
Louvre describes Hammurabi as king of Babylon.
The Met says that after Shamshi-Adad's death Hammurabi expanded control of the south and unified much of Mesopotamia.
The Met says Hammurabi destroyed King Zimri-Lim's palace at Mari on the Euphrates.
The page says Hammurabi’s forces defeated Mari in 1761 and describes the city as destroyed; it does not specify the palace destruction.
The mission says Tell Hariri is in the middle valley of the Syrian Euphrates and was identified as ancient Mari during the first excavation campaign in 1933.

evidence.locator: Excavations by André Parrot, paragraph 1 (page line 23)
evidence.note: The mission says thousands of tablets were found in the Great Royal Palace.
The Met describes a massive archive of cuneiform tablets at the palace as evidence for contemporary political events.

ISAC describes the book's focus on Old Babylonian education through House F in Nippur, excavated jointly by Chicago and Penn in the early 1950s and widely believed to be a scribal school; tablets document a curriculum.
The publication explicitly frames House F as a lens on education in the Old Babylonian period.
